House in Committee on Bill (No. 237) to amend the Civil Service Act.-The Postmaster General.
On section 1,

I would like to call the attention of the Postmaster General to another officer who, I think, might well be provided for under this section. There are provisions here for three of our deputy heads, the Deputy Minister of Justice, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals. There is a provision by which their salaries may be increased to $5,000, in certain events. The Deputy Minister of Justice, when appointed, must have had ten years' service at the bar. I can hardly imagine any man obtaining the position of Deputy Minister of Justice if he had served less than ten years at the bar, it would be very unusual ; and it looks to me as if this were rather a means of enabling this gentleman, and in tlie same manner these other two gentlemen, to get an exceptional allowance. Now I do not object, but I wish to bring forward the case of another official, the Auditor General. I am aware that there has been friction between the gentleman who holds that position and some of the other departments, but it seems to me that we should deal with the office, and that there should be no distinction made between the salary of a deputy minister of one of the departments and the salary of the Auditor General, at all events to' the disadvantage of the Auditor General. I do not think there is any deputy head in the whole service whose position is so important and so valuable to the country as that of the Auditor General. I cannot imagine that there is any sufficient reason why there should be any distinction between the salaries of the deputy heads I have named and that of an officer so important in the interests of the whole Dominion as the Auditor General. As I said before, I know there has been friction between the present incumbent of that office and other departments, probably I might more correctly say with the deputy heads of other departments. Well, I can only say that I doubt whether you will ever have an Auditor General, who attempts to do his duty, who will not have friction with the various departments. It is inevitable that it should be so. He is (lie criti-ciser, he is to a certain extent a fault-finder, and every time lie attempts to scrutinize the acts of the department he will meet with resistance ; if he persists there will

be more than resistance, there will be opposition. Now those of us who have read the correspondence in the Auditor General's Report know that he has come into conflict with deputy heads on matters that were likely to cause serious friction between them. Under those circumstances 1 think it is the duty of the government, instead of giving exceptional treatment to the deputy heads which will put him in a somewhat unfair position as regards rank, that they should protect the department of the Auditor General, whatever view they may take of the gentleman who occupies that office for the moment. 1 therefore suggest to the hon. the Postmaster General that it would be only proper, now that the salaries are being dealt with, to make provision in this section for the department of the Auditor General. lie is not a deputy head, he has not by statute the rank of deputy head, and he is apparently to be left out simply because lie has not D. H. after his name.

I appreciate what my hon. friend has said as to its being the duty of the government , to strengthen the hands of the Auditor General, to stand by him in the proper discharge of his duties, and to give proper weight and dignity to his high and responsible position I do not controvert anything the hon. gentleman has said as to the salary that should attach to the office, and if to-day I am not able to include his name in this list, it is not because of any decision to the contrary, either by the government or in my own mind. It may be that his case was not presented when the-cases of the deputy heads were under consideration. This Bill has grown, it has assumed proportions In excess of those that were contemplated when I introduced it. Therefore if the Auditor General is not being included with the others who are being given extra salaries, it is not because of any adverse conclusion we have come to, and no inference of that kind should be entertained. Perhaps my hon. friend would be good enough not to press the subject at this late date In the session. I think I can say on behalf of the government that, notwithstanding the supposed friction that has been referred to, the Auditor General enjoys the confidence and respect of the government, and we would be quite as ready as any hon. gentleman in the House to recognize his claims, both for increased emoluments and for support at the hands of the government in the discharge of his very embarrassing and responsible duties. Leaving the matter over for future consideration will not in any wise prejudice his claim. If we do not include him to-day it is simply because his case has not been under consideration. The Bill has grown, as I say, new clauses have been introduced from time to time. Under the circumstances this case might very properly come up for consideration at a later date.

I should be quite content with that decision, speaking for myself. But I would be better pleased if the Postmaster General would say that the case will be taken into consideration at an early date rather than at some future date. Some future date might be very far away. If it be that the Auditor General's case lias been overlooked, I hope the hon. gentleman will promise the House that it will be taken up at an early date, for consideration at all events. I am very glad to hear that the Auditor General has the confidence of the government. I believe the Auditor General has the confidence of the whole country and I am glad to hear now that the government do not disagree with the country in regard to him.

In asking that the matter be not pressed at this point, it was not for the purpose of shelving it indefinitely, but simply out of regard for the manifest desire of hon. members for an early prorogation. I wished to avoid anything that might interfere with that much desired end.
I see that the clause in regard to a civil engineer says that he must be a civil engineer of ten years' standing. What is the qualification of a civil engineer under that clause ?

The title of ' civil engineer ' may be acquired, I suppose without one having the diploma of an educational institution, but I think the construction that would be placed upon these words ' civil engineer ' in this case would be that they would apply to some person who had acquired the legal status of a civil engineer in a technical sense.
What is the legal status.

Perhaps it may be necessary that any one who sets himself up as a civil engineer is required to have a diploma from some college or university in civil engineering. There is a department of civil engineering in McGill and one at the School of Practical Science, Toronto. No government would consider a man as coming within the meaning of this section and being a civil engineer simply because he chose to call himself a civil engineer and sought to work in that way. He would have to be a civil engineer of standing and professionnal qualification evidenced either by the practice of his profession or by the diplomas of educational institutions. It seems to me there would be no difficulty in determining the meaning of the words ' civil engineer.'

Of course, I can understand that if he gets the diploma of a college or institution, such as the School

of Science, lie would come under this clause, but the great majority of those who are practising their professsion in this country have no diploma or anything beyond the fact that they are working at this profession. I think it ought to be defined.
I do not think that any government would recognize a man as a civil engineer under this section unless he had professional attainments and education to entitle him to such recognition.
This is making the government the interpreter of what a civil engineer is. The standard should be defined.

In reference to the matter raised by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) as to the position of the Auditor Genera!, I really feel as if the hon. minister in charge of this Bill has not given any satisfactory reason why the question should not be dealt with at this time. The hon. minister stated that this Bill had very largely developed in the course of its passage through the different stages.

I did not say so for the purpose of provoking discussion, but the very contrary. If my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) will reserve his observations to a later stage, I will let the Bill stand after the second reading, and then I will have an opportunity of consulting the government and perhaps be able to make an announcement.
All right.

I wish to add a few words to subsection (b) of section 2 of the Civil Service Act. The Clerk of the Privy Council is Mr. McGee. He is supposed to be the deputy head. He is called the deputy head, and he was supposed to come within the meaning of this section, but I cannot find any place in which he has been made deputy head by the statute. He is always included as a deputy head in the Civil Service list. Therefore, I propose to make the Civil Service Act meet the case by adding to this the following :
Subsection (b) of section 2 of the Civil Service Act is amended by inserting in the third line after the word ' department ' the words ' also the Clerk of the Privy Council.'
The committee will find by reference to subsection (b) of section 2 of the Civil Service Act, which I am now proposing to amend, that it says :
The expression ' deputy,' ' deputy head,' or ' deputy head of the department,' means the deputy of the minister of the Crown presiding over such department, and also includes the ' Auditor General,' in all cases in which such meaning is not inconsistent with his powers and duties under the ' Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act.'
Hon. Mr. HAGGART
I propose to add after the words ' head of the department,' a provision that it also includes the clerk of the Privy Council.

I would suggest that there are other officers, not perhaps of the government, but of this parliament, who fill positions apparently very similar to that of the Clerk of the Privy Council. I refer to the Chief Clerk of the House of Commons and to the Chief Clerk of the Senate. There are also the Librarians of Parliament.
They are going to be dealt with in another way.

I observe that, but it seems to me that provision should be made when we are passing this measure to see that the officers of the House of Commons do not receive worse treatment than those who fill other positions in the civil service. Since the hon. minister is making the amend! ment he is now making in favour of the Clerk of the Privy Council it would seem a simple and easy matter to include the Clerks of the House of Commons and the Senate.

I think that the fact that the Clerks of the House of Commons and Senate are officers of parliament should be a reason for their not being embraced in the Civil Service Act. They are outside of the Civil Service Act.

I understand the hon. minister to say that the Chief Clerk of the Senate and the Chief Clerk of the House of Commons are to be dealt with in another way. Will other officers of parliament be dealt with in the same way ? Is it the intention to deal only with the Chief Clerks of the two Houses or is it the intention to deal generally with the officers of the House of Commons ?
This is a section dealing with deputy heads. Would it not be advisable to dispose of this before we embark upon a general discussion upon another question ? I think we would make more progress.

I understand that this does not deal with the members of the staff of the House of Commons, but the hon. minister having referred to the Chief Clerk, I thought it was an opportune time to inquire about the balance of the staff of the House of Commons.

My remarks in reference to the Clerk of the House of Commons would apply to all officers of parliament. They are under the control of parliament in a different way from members of the civil service. They are not members of the civil service. This is a Bill to deal with the civil service, and if it is proposed to deal with the officers of parliament it should be done in a measure independently of the civil service.
Amendment agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, I move:
That section 2 be amended by striking out the words ' at the time of the coming into force o/ this Act ' in the 29th and 30th lines.
Amendment agreed to.

What is the meaning of the words in this section :	.
Either as deputy or in some other with capacity in the department.
The word ' with ' is a typographical error.
It must mean ' such '. capacity, or * like ' capacity.
No. It is only dealing with those in the public service at present, and if you strike out the word ' with ' it is all right.

This clause refers more particularly to the case of Mr. Gerald. He was for many years assistant commissioner, and for five or six years he discharged the duties of commissioner, Mr. Miall being ill. This is inserted in the Bill in order that Mr. Gerald may have the benefit of the increase the same as other deputy ministers.
It is retroactive ; giving him the benefit of the salary for five years past.
Yes.
Why didn't you come out and say so straight ?
In future, Mr. Gerald instead of being known as the commissioner, will be known as the deputy ?
Yes.
It only affects the salary henceforth.
He will be entitled to rank as deputy minister for five or six years past, so that he may get the increase of $100 a year, as the other deputy ministers get.
This clause is put in to give this gentleman a salary that he was not entitled to.
No, it gives him d record. He was acting practically as deputy minister during the illness of Mr, Miall for several years, and this is in order that his service for such should count.
Then you are paying two deputy ministers for some years.
We could have superannuated Mr, Miall.

You could fly if you had wings. You appear to have more consideration for these gentlemen than for the tax-payers. If any of these ministers were running their own business they would not do such a thing. This deputy minister was ill, and we all sympathize with him, and this other gentleman was not hurt at all by doing his work, but four or five years afterwards we have this kind of legislation coming down. The ministers do not give us an explanation that any ordinary mortal can understand, and we have to ply questions at them in order to grasp the situation. Now we are to pay two deputy ministers concurrently.
No.
What are you doing then ?
Does the hon. gentleman wish me to answer ?
Yes, if you give us some straight information and not mystify it.

I will try not to do that. We are not paying any back salary at all. We have here the case of one deputy who hais been in the service for a great many years, but prior to his appointment as deputy he had been performing the duties of the office, though not occupying the legal status of a deputy. It is now proposed to recognize his services to the extent of allowing his increase to commence at such amount as his length of service will entitle him to, instead of postponing it for some length of time.
He does not get any arrears ?

No. His increase will come in the future. If this session should ever come to an end, and this Bill becomes law, then this deputy minister will be eligible for this increase, so that every day we are protracting the session we are keeping that increase back.
I would suggest to the ministers that they should give plain explanations and not be constantly mystifying what they say.
The word ' with ' in the clause has no meaning.
It must have been intended for the word ' such,' so as to read, ' some other such capacity.'
I do not think that is necessary at all.
It certainly is necessary if you read the context.

I am afraid the Auditor General might hold that although acting as deputy and not having the status of a deputy, it would not be such capacity as would entitle this officer to I come in under the terms of the section. So

far as I know, there is only one deputy in the service to whom these words apply ; the whole section is limited to men who are in the service and who are well known. Therefore no great grievance can grow out of it. Every person who has now the legal status of a deputy will come in under this section, if you pass it.
I cannot see how anyone would he affected injuriously if you added the words, ' or some such capacity.' Under the Bill, a man might act in some other capacity. He might be a messenger.
There is no such case.	.
But if there were such a ease, this would apply to it, and it would make it absurd, because service in such a capacity would certainly be of no value in determining the man's salary.

Suppose we adopted the hon. gentleman's suggestion, the Auditor General might say that as a matter of law he could not recognize that Mr. Gerald, who was serving in the capacity of assistant commissioner, was taking the place of the deputy; and therefore he would not come within this provision.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.	[DOT]
On section 4-certain salaries not affected.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved that after the word ' salary ' in the first line, the words ' or emolument ' be inserted.
What does that mean V

It happens that some of the deputies receive something outside of their salaries. For example, Mr. Parmelee, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce, gets an allowance as controller of Chinese, and Mr. McDougald, Commissioner of Customs, besides his salary of $2,800, receives $800 as Chairman of the Board of Appraisers. These extra fees may be considered as emoluments, and it is not proposed to take them away. We want to allow the officers to retain whatever they have now.

We have here an example of legislation brought down by a minister of the crown in such a crude state that the time of this committee has to be taken up whipping it into shape. There has hardly been a Bill introduced by the government this session that has not had to be amended over and over again before it lias been in a shape to carry out the intention. This proves to me as a layman that the legislation is not properly considered before it is brought to this House. I think the country might better pay a competent draftsman to find out what the ministers mean, and then to put their legislation in such a shape as to carry out their intention. We

have a provision here in regard to Mr. Parmelee, an official in a department which the minister who presides over it used to say was a sinecure and should never have been created. The hon. minister's soul is not now harassed by the fact that the farmers are being bled white. The hon. gentleman's deputy minister is receiving the same salary as he did in those days and now the minister proposes to increase it or rather to have the obnoxious word ' emolument ' or ' allowance' removed and have it made a salary so that when the minister leaves his present position the deputy will have the full salary. The hon. minister we know is idle and the deputy must be idle too and lie wishes to leave him in a secure position.
1 understand that my hon. friend wants to have a law clerk appointed to do this work. That is a subject worthy of consideration but we would not care to add to the burdens of the taxpayers now.

I know how much you are concerned about the taxpayers, when you have all the offices loaded with officials and the taxpayers are not considered at all. If 5rou had officials that had some brains to do this work that would be a benefit and we would not be detained here as we have been. The hon. gentleman brings down a measure and the moment a section is read he says he will have to amend it. How could a layman like myself understand that Bill ?
Oh, oh !
I am serious about it. I do not think it is anything to laugh at that we are here from day to day.
I hope that ' Hansard ' will not include the speech of my hon. friends as part of my own.
They have been deceived enough, with what you said in parliament without transferring anything I said to your credit.

I do not think it would be fail- to take away the allowances which these old officers have had and to reduce them ; that is the point. We want to protect them in their rights. Whether it was right or not in days gone by to make these allowances is another matter, but I think the committee will agree that we should protect them in their rights.

I have no objection to protecting them in their rights. I said nothing about their rights. The Postmaster General should not put in my mouth words that I did not use. This would not excuse the Postmaster General for what he said year after year when we proposed to give anything to the civil service. He was one of the first on his feet with the Minister of

Customs denouncing the extravagance of the Tory party. The Minister of Trade and Commerce used to wax eloquent and his soul was torn with the burden we were placing on the farmers and now we are voting millions of money.
Sections as amended, agreed to.
Progress reported.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.
On section 5,
This Act shall not apply to the present Deputy of the Minister of Justice until the conclusion of his present engagement as one of the commissioners for the revision of the Statutes of Canada.
This is because the Deputy Minister of Justice gets an allowance in connection with the revision of the statutes.
Besides his salary as deputy minister and the allowance in connection with this revision of the statutes, I think he has another allowance, though I have forgotten what it is.

I do not know as to that. At all events he has recently been appointed commissioner for revising the statutes for which he will get an allowance. It is not intended to give him the benefit of this Act until his com-missionership ends.	.
On section 6,
Section 13 of the Civil Service Act is repealed and the following section is substituted therefor :-
13. The deputy head of each department shall, subject to the directions of the head of the department, oversee and direct the officers, clerks and employees in the department, and shall have general control of the business thereof, and shall perform such other duties as are assigned to him by the Governor in Council. He shall give his full time to the public service and shall discharge all duties required by the head of the department, or by the Governor in Council, whether such duty is in his own department or not ; and no deputy head shall receive any bay, fee or allowance in any form in excess of the amount provided for him in section 12 of this Act.
This section is to exclude claims for any other service.
The preceding section makes it clear, I suppose, without any exception being mentioned in this section, that the Deputy Minister of Justice is not included ?

Yes.
On section 7,
7. In addition to the class of chief clerkships referred to in sections 15 and 16 of the said
Act, another class, to be known as that of ' chief clerkship, grade A,' is hereby created.
2.	The minimum salary paid to a chief clerk, grade A, shall be two thousand four hundred dollars per annum, with annual increases of one hundred dollars up to a maximum of two thousand eight hundred dollars per annum.
3.	A chief clerk in any department may be promoted to grade A, by an Order in Council passed after-
(a.) The deputy head has reported that the duties devolving upon such officer are of special importance, and that the officer recommended for such promotion is specially qualified for their performance ;
(b.) The concurrence of the head of the department in such report ; and
(c.) The salary has been voted by parliament.
(d.) If a person on appointment to a chief clerkship, grade A, is at the time of such appointment in receipt of a salary greater than the minimum salary of such chief clerkship as above provided, he may be appointed to such chief clerkships at the salary he is then in receipt of, provided it does not exceed the maximum salary of such chief clerkship a3 above provided.
[ move to amend subsection 3 so as to read: ' A chief clerk in any department may, without being required to undergo any special or other examination be promoted to grade A ' &e.
Amendment agreed to.

Is a clerk promoted to a chief clerkship, grade A., to have his salary increased over whatever he may be receiving ? For example, if his class entitled him to a maximum of $1,800, but his actual salary is $2,000, would you make the Increases to $2,100, $2,200 and so on ?

This section is limited solely to chief clerks in grade A, and does not cover all chief clerks. A man promoted to grade A enters me class at a minimum salary of $2,400. If he had been in receipt of $2,400 for a year before that promotion, he would be eligible for an increase of $100. But if he had been in receipt of $2,400 for less than a year, his increase would not begin until the expiry of a year from his last increase.

Suppose he had been receiving $2,600 instead of $2,400. Would he then receive $2,700, being an increase of $100 over his then salary, or $2,500, being an increase of $100 over the minimum of his class ?
Such a case could not arise. A man will be transferred from a lower class to grade A, and at promotion he would receive $2,400 as a minimum.
How many did you intend this to apply to ?

Nothing has been settled in that way. I do not think the ministers have gone through their departments with that view. I have not gone

through mine. When a law like this is to apply generally, it is impossible in advance to go through and make your selection.
It cannot apply until next session, because parliament has to vote the money.

No, it is not arranged in that way. If you would allow' me, Mr. Chairman, to direct the attention of my bon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) for purposes of explanation to section 2(5, he will And that after referring to moneys voted by parliament, it provides :
And during the financial year ending on the thirtieth day of June, 1904, there may he paid from out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as have been voted by parliament but are required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.
There are conditions in the Bill such as are found in the Civil Service Act, that, before a chief clerkship can be created, there must be an Order in Council, a recommendation by the deputy head and concurrence by the head of the department.

It seems to me the government ought to be prepared to give the House some information as to the number w'ho will be affected by this reorganization. Some one must have gone through and made some sort of calculation. If we have not that information, we do not know what expense the country is being committed to by this change. I assume that every one of these will want to be promoted at the earliest possible moment after this Act passes.

They are not all at their maximum, comparatively few are at their maximum now'. I have no doubt that there will be a certain number of promotions, and they will be made prizes to be sought after. Instead of dumping the whole number into the higher class, all who might by law' be put there, the government will exercise a careful discretion. They are treated as privates, and this is simply an intermediate step between the chief clerk and a deputy.
I suppose it is because tlie deputy heads do not die quick enough.

No, but it makes a smaller step. It is an incentive to service, so that a man should not feel that he has got to the end of his career because he has got to the maximum of a chief clerk, and that there is still a prize beyond that point.
What sum of money is available from the votes of parliament for this purpose ?

It is not possible to say, because at present there are eligible cases all through the service, and unless we have an omnibus clause such Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
as clause 26, it will be necessary to revote the whole salary for every man who is promoted from a chief clerkship to grade A. Under the section, any payment of salary to a man as chief clerk should be available to pay that same man if he is transferred to the higher class. Otherwise you would have to go through the whole service and revote all that is voted for the chief clerkships.
I understood there was to be a provision inserted in section 7 to apply the same rule to the Auditor General's Department.

I have an amendment for that purpose now'. I move to add this subsection to section 7 :
The provisions of subsection 3, section 24, of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, as that section is enacted by section 1 of chapter 16 of the statutes of 1891, shall apply to promotions to chief clerkships in grade A in the office of the Auditor General.
That is in order that the Auditor General should have the same control over promotions to grade A as he has in regard to promotions of other members of his staff. Since we are speaking of the Auditor General, I find it won't be possible for me to settle that particular question in; time for the present measure. The session is so far advanced that I find it impossible to take up anything new, or to indulge in any departure or amendment that will involve any delay. So I think it will be wiser to leave the matter as it is with the expressions that have fallen from hon. gentlemen, until next session.
Will the minister leave all the promotions to the Auditor General ?
Whatever they are under the Audit Act; we do not propose any change.
This section which is proposed will give him the same power precisely with respect to grade A that he already has w'ith clerks in his department, neither more nor less.
Precisely.

Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section (a),

This clause merely re-echoes the resolutions that passed, increasing the; minimum and maximum by $100. Section 16 fixes the minimum of a chief clerkship at $1,800 and the maximum at $2,400. This adds $100 at each end.
On section 14,
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved to amend by adding as subsection 2 the following :

Subsection 2 of section 39 ot the Civil Service Act is amended by striking out the word only ' in the second line and by inserting the following words : ' and at such other time as may be from time to time fixed by the Governor in Council.'
Section 39 of the Civil Service Act provides that promotion examinations shall be held only once a year, in the month of May. It is rather inconvenient to have Only one time in the year at which to hold promotion examinations, therefore it is proposed, not to dispense with the promotion examination in May, but to hold promotion examinations at other times in addition, when desirable.
Can a supplemental examination be held at any time by one member of the board or must it be held by the whole board ?
No, it is held by Order in Council. It is really a departmental, technical examination. It is not an examination for the public, but for those actually in the service.
It gives the government power to hold a special examination between times.
Yes, more than once a year.
You can order a special examination for any candidate for a position ?
Yes.
Had you not that power before ?
No, the statute says only once a year.

Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 17,
Is that a substitute clause for the one that is at present in the Civil Service Act ?

At present there are no third-class clerks except those who are appointed before the repeal of the provision for third-class clerks. I think that under the Act they were eligible for $50 a year increase. We are restoring the old annual increase of $50. The class that took the place of the third-class, the temporary writers, began at $400, and they had only an annual increase of $30 a year.

But my point is this : The parties who were appointed to be third-class clerks before that class was abolished claim that they had the right to their increment of $50 a year. Of course that question was threshed out in the House and Sir Charles Tupper, while leader of the opposition, took strong ground that it was a statutory right they obtained upon appointment. This does not make it a statutory right but leaves it optional with the government.
This does not alter the law.

It is just a doubtful point whether it alters the law or not.
On section 19,
Any person who is now, or hereafter may be, writer, clerk, packer, sorter, or messenger, temporary or otherwise, in the service of the government of Canada, employed in one of the departments at Ottawa, or in the office of the Auditor General, may, under Order in Council, be appointed a third-class clerk at a salary not less than the salary of which he was in receipt or to which he would be entitled at the time of such appointment (but limited always to a sum not exceeding to maximum salary of the third class); provided always that any such person, who in the capacity aforesaid, or in any other capacity, has been continuously in the said service for two years prior to the passing of this Act, may be so appointed without regard to his age and without passing the qualifying examination. and the said Order in Council shall be held to create the third-class clerkship in respect of which such appointment is made, and the Governor in Council may, in the case of any such person whose salary is at the time of his appointment as third-class clerk less than five hundred dollars a year, increase such salary to five hundred dollars a year, but no such increase shall take effect from a date prior to the date of the coming into force of this Act, nor shall it be made except on the report of the deputy head of the department, concurred in by the head of the department, that such clerk is deserving thereof.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved that :
Section 19 be amended by inserting after the word ' who ' in the first line the words ' either before or after the passing of this Act was or who thereafter ' and striking out the words ' is now or hereafter '; also to insert the letter (a) after the word 'be' on the first line; and in the 30th and following lines to strike out the words * but no such increase shall take effect from a date prior to the date of the coming into-force of this Act, nor shall it be made except.'
He said : This does not change the legal effect. The Act will come into operation when it receives the royal assent, and these words are therefore unnecessary.
This virtually does away with the civil service examination for third-class clerks, because it allows anyone who has been in tbe service to be appointed to that grade without examination.
It provides that those who have been in the service for two years in a temporary capacity as packers, sorters, messengers, &c., shall not have to undergo an examination.
After this amendment has been passed, who will be required to pass the examination 1

Those who have been in the service for two years prior to the first

of July, 1003, as packers, sorters or messengers in a temporary capacity may be promoted to tile third-class without regard to age, and without having to pass an examination.
Hon. Mr. HAGGAItT. Does this give power to make a third-class clerk, even if there is no vacancy ?	[DOT]
No question of a vacancy would arise in the beginning, and this does not dispense with the examination for any person who is hereafter appointed.
It only applies to those who have been two years in the service ?

Or who hereafter may be in the service as temporaries for two or three years. The temporaries can look forward to being transferred to the third-class as a reward. The question of vacancies would not arise at the beginning, because there will be no third-class clerkships in existence when this Act goes into effect. The old third-class clerkship has been merged into the junior second, so that to-day we have to start by promoting the temporaries into the third class. My own opinion is that we ought to make a liberal use of this provision, and transfer the temporaries into the third class clerkships as they show themselves deserving. A temporary position, with from $500 to $600 a year, is not a satisfactory position to hold in the service of the Dominion, and so far as my department is concerned I would look forward with pleasure to being able to go through the department, and to select all who are deserving of being made permanent. That is the spirit in which I would feel myself bound to interpret it.
Do you, by Order in Council, create the third-class clerkships ? That was the question of the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) ?

The hon. member for Lanark spoke of vacancies, and I explained to him that the question of vacancies would arise. My own department is constantly expanding, and it is impossible to tell parliament with any accurate detail, the number of temporary writers you will require throughout the year ; you have to feel your way into it. Probably in one month you will find your staff inadequate to cope with the increased number of post office savings bank acccounts and other work, and you have to make a temporary appointment under the law. I would look forward to that temporary appointee becoming permanent, if he were fit for the position. We may consider that most positions in the service are of a permanent character; they certainly are in the Post Office Department. When a man is employed temporarily and proves himself de-
serving, he ought to be put on the permanent list and have a chance to rise in the service.

Under the present Act it requires the deputy minister to report as to the necessities of the department, and the minister to concur in tLat report, and the council to approve of the organization set out in that report, before parliament is asked to vote the sums necessary to provide for the organization of that department. This clause would appear to give power to the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the minister, to appoint any number of third-class clerks.
Not after this fiscal year.

It certainly inter-[DOT] feres with the existing Act in that respect. After all, I look upon our civil service examination as at present conducted as a sort of farce, and especially the examination for promotion from one class to another. A man who is at the maximum of the second class for thirteen or fourteen years, cannot be promoted to the first-class because he cannot pass some technical examination which is not pertinent at all to his office. I place very little faith in the civil service examination, but I think the minister should go through the form with regard to the organization as required by the existing Act.

The observations of my hon. friend, if applied generally, are very fair, but he will see that the promotion to the third class is limited to the number we have at present in a temporary capacity, and I hope the government will make a liberal use of this power.

Section 40 of the Civil Service Act provides :
Once in each year, and not later than the 15th day of March, the deputy head of each department shall make and lay before the board, through the Department of the Secretary of State, an estimate of the number of vacancies likely to occur during the ensuing year.	>
Then it names certain grades in reference to which this report is to be made.
This clause does away with that altogether, so that that is not applicable to this clause.

It is applicable in this sense, that the only time when an estimate can be -made of the number of clerks required in the department is once a year, on the report prepared under the provisions of section 40.

I desire to bring to the notice of the hon. Minister of Labour the case of Mr. H. W. Mutch, who has been a messenger for the Marine and Fisheries Department, in Mr. Lord's office at Charlottetown for the last ten years, at $20 a month. If the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries were in his place, I might get

some information from him in that regard. We are all proud of the civil service of Canada. In every department, from the deputy head down to the lowest clerk, they are a credit to Canada, and are equal to any body of civil servants in any other part of the world.

Would my hon. fi^end allow me to make a suggestion ? I am not familiar with the case to which he refers, but there will be an item in the estimates connected with the Department of Marine and Fisheries when the minister of that department will be present. If my hon. friend will bring the matter up then, it would be more satisfactory.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what examination the old employees will have to undergo ; for instance, men who have 'been working for the government for fifteen or twenty years ?

My hon. friend is referring to the Department of Customs. His question will be answered by subsection 3 of section 37, which provides that the examination hereafter shall be upon the duties of the office, and be departmental rather than the ordinary civil service examination.

I agree that in certain departments, such as the Customs Department, a civil service examination is out of the question. Take landing waiters, lockers and checkers, who check goods passing from steamers into cars ; these men have special training for special work, and I think it would be very unfair and ridiculous to ask them to pass a civil service examination.

What will be the effect of section 6 of the Civil Service Act provided this passes ? That section says :
The Governor in Council shall, from time to time, determine the number of officers, chief clerks, clerks, messengers and other employees required for the working of the several departments.
Then it goes on to provide that all others shall be supernumerary clerks without being eligible for increase of salary. That is practically the skeleton of your service. I do not see any clause in this Bill which repeals that ; and if it is not repealed, it seems to me that you cannot by Order in Council add the third-class clerkship again.
This Act must prevail over all prior Acts. When it says the Governor in Council can create an additional third-class clerkship, it must take the place of any prior legislation that clashes with it.
I do not think that is a very proper way to pass legislation. It seems to me that section 6 will have some force and effect if it is not specifically repealed.

I do not say that section 6 of the Civil Service Act is repealed entirely and actually ; but it is repealed pro tanto, so far as those now in the service are concerned. This is to start the new class going, 'but when this fiscal year runs out the full force of section 6 will apply.
Mr.. SPROULE. If it only applied to those now in the service I could understand it, but you provide for those who may come in in the future.

There can be no appointment without a vote of money. This Bill does not dispense with the voting of money specifically, except for the remainder of this year and with respect to those now in the service. When this fiscal year expires there wifi be so many third-class clerkships, and the estimates for future years must be voted in the same way as heretofore.
But you are practically creating another class by Order in Council.

A government would not create a clerkship if it had not money to pay the clerk. There can be practically no appointment made until parliament votes the money.
On section 20,
What is the effect of this ?
This section does not alter the Civil Service Act of 1887. It classifies the employees under three classes, while now they are all enumerated in one list.
Does it increase the salaries ?

No, it does not make any change in that way; it simply puts them in groups.
On section 21,
In section 37 of the Act of 1887 there was a subclause B ; that is left out.
That is the clause providing that an appointment shall be made from outside the service only if no person in the civil service has the qualifications for the office.

We left that out for this reason :	Suppose that in
the Customs Department you want an appraiser, a techincal officer, and you have a man in the customs service who is possessed of the qualifications required ; you cannot appoint him, because the deputy has to certify that the requisite qualifications are not possessed by any person then in the service, and it may be a preventive officer, who has the qualifications and he



cannot give that certificate. Therefore we have left out the words :
Said appointments shall be made from the civil service if any person therein shall he found available.
Subsection 3 is entirely new, and is added to section 37. This is to meet a difficulty that was discussed when the customs estimates were under consideration, and I think the provision now made meets the wishes of members on both sides of the House. We have a great many old officers in the outside department of the service who have been engaged in the work for years and years, but who hesitate to attempt the literary examination, if I may call it so, that the Civil Service Act requires, and yet we consider that they are very competent officers in the discharge of their duties. But still, as they have not passed the examination, we have either to appoint them preventive officers, which is too general, or they have to remain on the temporary list. It is desirable I think in the public interest and in their interest, that they should be made permanent officers, and by this section you dispense with the literary examination pre scribed by the Civil Service Act so far as the outside service is concerned, and substitute therefor a technical practical examination on the duties of their office which they will be able to pass.

What changes does this make? The Minister of Customs said a moment ago that this would not affect salaries, but was simply putting them into classes ; but I see that it increases the salaries of a number of classes. Perhaps the Minister of Customs will explain that when he returns to the House.
On section 22,
So much of schedule (b) to the Civil Service Act as is included under the heading 1 Inland Revenue,' as enacted by section 3 of chapter 12 of the statutes of 1889, is repealed, and the following is substituted therefor :-

To which may be added for surveys of important manufactories an additional salary, for the special class excisemen and other officers connected with the survey, not exceeding in any one case two hundred dollars per annum.
Is this clause intended to apply in the future as in the past ? It seems to me that you are extra liberal to these people.

I will explain that. With regard to the special class excisemen, we have been in the habit of paying additional salary because the hours of work are 1 singer and because the work is special and highly technical. The clause remains the same with regard to that addition of salary to which may be added for service of important manufactories an additional salary for tlie special class excisemen, who perform that duty, not exceeding $100 per annum. But, as very often the work cannot be performed by one man, who is the chief officer in the distillery, we have had it revised so that the class will be :
To which may be added for surveys of Important manufactories an additional salary for the special excisemen class and other officers connected with such survey, not exceeding in any one case two hundred dollars per annum.
But I have similar officers to these in distilleries, one man cannot perform the duties alone, and he has what is called an assistant, who may not be a special class officer, but an officer of tlie first or second class, which is next to the rank of first officer, be should receive an additional salary of not over $200 when he is in charge of these distilleries. But this salai-y is paid only to those officers who work in those distilleries and serve long hours.
Do you think they are of more importance than the deputy collectors, who only get $1,700, that you give these men $2,000 ?

Yes. The responsibility is very much greater. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) knows that the most important part of the revenue is derived from the distilleries, and we must have a special class of men, men of technical knowledge. I regard the special class officers as the most Important in the service-even more important than the collector or inspector of the division. They must possess technical knowledge which cannot be learned in a few years, and they must work for years, besides passing an examination of two or three classes before they reach that position.
Do not the deputy collectors require the same knowledge ?

Oh, no. The position of deputy collector is open for almost everybody. They do not have to pass any examination, and their responsibility is not great, because the collector is responsible. Of course, lie may take charge in case of the collector's sickness or absence, but be is not otherwise responsible. And he need not have technical

skill equal to that of the special class excise officer.

I understood that the hon, member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) had called attention, while I was out for a moment, to a mistake I had made in saying that there had been no increase in salary. I did not allow for the effect of the classification. For instance, under this Bill tide surveyors are classed with chief landing waiters and chief lockers. The old Bill being chief landing waiters and chief lockers, $1,200, that being voted, and tide surveyors being credited with that, gives them the same,	and to that extent I was
wrong. And the messengers get $100 increase to the maximum. That is a change, I think, since I gave the Bill consideration. When I spoke I was under the impression that it made no change and hon. members will see that the change is very slight.
The Bill does not make any difference between deputies in the first-class divisions and other divisions.
The salary is not mentioned here, but it is fixed by the minister himself. The minimum is $500 and the maximum $1,700, according to the importance of the division.
The hon. minister thinks the duty of the deputy collector in a first-class division is almost equal to the duty of a special excise officer attending a distillery ?

I always considered the duties of a special officer unique. They are quite different from any other service performed by any other officer in the department. Of course, the salary of $1,700 is paid only in large divisions like Montreal and Toronto, on account of the responsibility upon the collector and upon his assistant. It has always been left to the minister to determine what shall be the salaries of the deputy collectors. There are two classes, classes A and B, and each man is paid according to the importance of the work he has under his charge.
On section 23,
The Governor in Council may grant such increases of salary in the Departments of Customs and Inland Revenue as are by this Act authorized, but no such increase shall take effect from a date prior to the date of the coming into force of this Act, nor shall it be made except upon the report of the deputy head of the department, concurred in by the head of the department, that the person recommended for such increase is deserving thereof.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL moved to amend by striking out the words 'but no such increase shall take effect from a date prior to the date of the coming into force of this Act, nor shall it be made except '.

If you have a vote for the salary, and you are not limited to the 433J
date of the passage of this Act, why would it not be good for the current year ?
That will be for the Department of Justice to determine. But if we pass the Act now and it goes into effect on a certain date, I do not know how you can make it retroactive.
What is the object of striking out these words ?

Section 27 of the Bill says the Act shall go into effect on the 1st of July, 1903, and unless these words in section 23 had been inserted, it would have been possible, with section 27 standing, to have made the salary commence at the date when the Act came into force. But by striking out section 27 you must also strike out the corresponding safeguard that .runs through the Bill. By not saying that the Act shall come into effect on the 1st of July but only allowing it to come into effect when it becomes law, then it is necessary to provide that the salary shall not begin at an anterior date.

I am of the opinion the hon. gentleman is right as to his conclusion, but you would require either express words or necessary implication in order to give the Act retroactive effect. But I do not follow the line of his argument exactly. It does not seem to me these words are any less necessary now than they were before-I refer to the words which are being struck out. I do not see that striking out section 27 affects this either one way or the other. All you say in section 23 is that no increase shall take effect from a date prior to the date of the coming into force of this Act. It does not seem to me to make any difference.

To make the point I had in my mind I should have said ' Prior to the passing of the Act.' However, what I intended was to prevent a retroactive effect of the law and to let it take effect when it receives the royal assent.
I would be inclined to think that the hon. Postmaster General is right about that, and I think the original words in section 23 were introduced because of a possibly erroneous idea of section 27.

Quite so.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 26,
All sums of money voted by parliament for the financial year ending on the thirtieth day of June, 1904, for the payment of the salaries or the increases to the salaries of any persons now in the public service, shall, in the event of the promotion of any such persons to higher classes or grades, or on their transfer to other positions in the public service, or their becoming entitled to, or being granted, increases of salary under the provisions of this Act, be applicable in or towards payment of the salaries or in-

creases to the salaries of such persons so promoted or transferred, or becoming entitled to or being granted increases as aforesaid ; and during the financial year ending on the thirtieth day of June, 1904, there may be paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as have been voted by parliament but are required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.

That section 26 be amended by inserting after the words ' nineteen hundred and four ' in the second line the words 'and applicable'; also by striking out the word * now ' in the 4th line and by inserting the word ' not' after the word ' have ' in the 3rd line from the last of the clause. .
That gives you au opportunity of going into the treasury when you had no authority to go into it before. You can only deal with what has been voted.

This allows the government to apply the moneys which have been voted and are now applicable to the payment of the salaries of officers although they are transferred to a higher class. Take for example the case of a chief clerk. If a chief clerk were promoted to grade A the money that we have already voted to pay the salary as a chief clerk would be available to pay him although he was transferred to a higher class. Take the class of temporary writers. There are in the service of the Post Office Department alone about one hundred of this class. The sums for this class have been voted heretofore in bulk simply under the heading of contingencies and they will be available for this class for the present fiscal year although the temporary class have ceased to be temporaries and have become third-class clerks. At the end of this year, when we enter upon a new fiscal year, they will appear in the ordinary way under the old practice and hereafter a vote will be taken for them as clerks and not as a part of the contingencies of the department.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
That section 27 be struck out.

Motion agreed to.
Progress reported.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolutions :
1.	Resolved., that the salaries ot the general librarian and the parliamentary librarian ot the library ot parliament. [DOT] and the registrar ot the Supreme Court of Canada shall each be $3,500 per annum ; with an annual increase of $100, up to a maximum ot $4,000 per annum.
2.	Resolved, that for the purpose of determining the salary of the officers at present occupying

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext:
the said positions, each shall be credited with his period of service ; and shall hereafter be paid such salary as he would by length of service have become entitled to, had the provision of the next preceding resolution been in force at the time of his appointment.
3.	Resolved, that during the financial year ending June 30, 1904, there may be paid, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, such sums as are required for payment of the foregoing increases. -The Minister of Justice.

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext: What are their salaries now ?

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext:
Chapter 15 of the Revised Statutes, ' an Act respecting the Library of Parliament,' section 4 provides that there shall be two officers, one of whom shall be called the general librarian and the other of whom shall be called the parliamentary librarian, which officers shall be appointed by joint commission, under the Great Seal, as librarians of parliament, and shall have equal powers as respects the control and management of the library. Section 5 provides that the salary of each officer so appointed shall be such sum not exceeding $3,000 as the Governor in Council directs. Under section 0 it is provided that:
The general librarian, parliamentary librarian, and other officers and servants of the library of parliament, shall be responsible for '.he faithful discharge of their official duties, as the same are defined by regulations agreed upon by the Speakers of the two Houses, and concurred in by the said joint committee on the library.
These gentlemen are really officers of parliament and do not come under the Civil Service Act properly so-called.

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext: That will bring each of the librarians up to the limit of the statute ?

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext: This is in accordance with suggestions which, I think, were made at the time when the Bill providing for the increase of certain salaries was before the Committee of the House, that the librarians of parliament had some right to be considered in connection with it.

maintopic: SALARIES OF PARLIAMENTARY LIBRARIANS AND REGISTRAR OF SUPREME COURT.
speechtext: Then that brings them up at once to $4,000 ?

speechtext:
I wish to call attention to the fact that the clerks of the House of Commons and the staff of the House of Commons generally, are, so far as I can understand, not included at all in the legislation that has passed this House, and are not going to derive any advantage through it.
I would suppose that it would be advisable that the officers of the House of Commons should participate in the benefits of the present movement to increase the salaries generally speaking of the servants of the country. It would seem somewhat extraordinary if the House of Comons were providing for every, one else to the exclusion of those who are more particularly their own officials. I understand that the Senate is much more liberal in dealing with its staff than is the House of Commons, but I would like to know from the Minister of Justice, if it is necessary to pass legislation in order that the staff of the House of Commons, and the staff of the Senate may participate in these advantages ? If so, this would be an opportune time to add to this resolution, so as to include the members of the House of Commons staff. I am sure that generally speaking, the members of the House of Commons would like to see the legislation so extended as to include the officers of this House.

On amendment 1,

The first amendment is to section 2, subsection (b). At present it reads as follows :
The expression 'by-law' includes a resolution.

On amendment 2,

The second amendment Is to section 5, for which the Senate proposes to substitute the following :
Every railway, steam or electric street railway or tramway, the construction or operation of which is authorized by a special Act passed by the legislature of any province, now or hereinafter connecting with or crossing a railway which, at the time of such connection or crossing, is subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, is hereby declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada in respect only to such connection or crossing or to through-traffic thereon or anything appertaining thereto, and also to the provisions set forth in this Act relating to offences and penalties, navigable waters and criminal matters, and this Act shall apply to that extent only.
2. This section shall not, however, operate as regards through-traffic on railways owned by any provincial government, without the consent of such government.
Then, they leave out sections 6 and 7 altogether. That is to say, we are to depart from the principle which we have adopted and which has been in force for many years, that parliament declares a work to he for the general advantage of Canada, and not simply a piece of the work. I can see no good reason why we should adopt a new prlnciule which it seems to me would be of doubtful legality and a very serious inconvenience in the operation of the road.
What was the object of the amendment ?

The object of the amendment, as I understand it,

is that instead of declaring the whole work to be for the general advantage of Canada, and as a result of that declaration bringing the whole railway within our jurisdiction, we should exercise our jurisdiction only with respect to that particular portion of the railway which is connected with the crossing.
The hon. gentleman does not propose to concur in this amendment.

On amendment 3,

By the third amendment it is proposed to leave out section 6, and by the fourth amendment to leave out section 7. These two sections are necessary if section 5 is retained, and therefore I propose to disagree with respect to those two for the same reason as in the case of the second amendment.

I quite concur in the view of the hon. Minister of Justice and I might have some other reasons in addition to those which he has already pointed out, although these reasons are, perhaps, more a question of legislative wisdom than of constitutional validity. I do not see how you could work out the provision that a railway in respect to its connection with or crossing by another railway should be a work for the general advantage of Canada and in respect to other things should not be a work for the general advantage of Canada ; and I do not see how a railway _ shall be a provincial railway, that is not for the general advantage of Canada with respect to all local traffic, but for the general advantage of Canada as to through-traffic. I think that, in addition to what the Minister of Justice has suggested, it would be absolutely impracticable to work out the provision suggested in the Senate. I have not had the advantage, however, of hearing or reading the arguments that has been adduced in support of their views.

I read with some care what was said in the Senate and I think the object the Senate had in view was to prevent the parliament of Canada extending its jurisdiction to local railways. The intention was to limit our jurisdiction as far as possible. Now, that intention may be very good but it seems to me that with respect to this particular class of enterprise it is most desirable that railways which connect together should he under tue same jurisdiction.

Having regard as to whether the right to one or more crossings or to take away or withhold rights of crossing formed part of the consideration paid by the company to the landowner, or of the bargain by which the company acquired the land.

The amendment of the Senate would have the effect of unduly limiting the discretion of the board while we contend that it is proper that the board should have absolute discretion in the premises to determine whether an additional farm crossing is necessary. I therefore beg to move :
That the said amendment be not concurred in for the reason that the amendment unduly limits the discretion of the board of commissioners.
Then you propose to leave it entirely in the hands of the commissioners as to whether they shall give an additional crossing to a portion of a farm ?
Yes, in ease a farm is subdivided.
I think the farmer should have that right without being obliged to apply to the board for it.

Section 198 provides that:
Every company shall make crossings for persons across whose lands the railway is carried, convenient and proper for the crossing of the railway for farm purposes. In crossing with live stock, the same shall be in charge of some competent person, who shall use all reasonable care and precaution to avoid accidents.
That is the law as we have it at the present time, but when the farm is subdivided the question arises as to whether each subdivision of the farm is entitled to a crossing. In a case in the Supreme Court against the Grand Trunk Railway Company it was decided that the original crossing was the only crossing that was binding on the company and that the subdivision of the farm afterwards did not entitle the man who got the subdivided farm Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
to an additional erosssiug. This provision of the new Bill is to enable tlie man who has acquired the subdivided farm to go before the board and let the board decide whether an additional crossing is necessary or not. The intention of the Senate is to limit the authority of the board by providing that the board shall be obliged to take into account all the conditions existing at the time the right to the farm crossing was acquired. We think it proper not to bind it in this respect but to allow the board to determine what shall lie done under the existing conditions at the time the application is made.

The Senate amendment means, that, where a party sells his land to a railway company and makes a bargain with the railway company that he shall not. have more than oue crossing, or that he shall not have any crossing, notwithstanding that bargain, be may apply to the board for the purpose of securing a crossing.

It is just the other way about. Subsection 2 of the Bill reads as follows :
The board may, upon the application of any landowner, order the company to provide and construct a suitable farm crossing across the railway, wherever in any case the board deems it necessary for the proper enjoyment of his land, on either side of the railway, and safe in the public interest ; and may order and direct how, when, where, by whom, and upon wh5t terms and conditions, such farm crossing shall be constructed and maintained.
This leaves it absolutely under the control of the commissioners to determine whether or not an additional farm crossing is advisable. The Senate leave these words I have just read as they were originally, but they add this paragraph :
Having regard as to whether the right to one or more crossings or to take away or withhold rights of crossings formed part of the consideration paid by the company to the landowner, or-of the bargain by which the company acquired the land.
Under this amendment the commissioners are obliged, in determining whether or not they shall grant an additional farm crossing, to consider the terms of the contract under which the railway company acquired the land from the original landowner in connection! with which land application for a farm crossing is being made.
I-Ion. Mr. HAGGART. It is exactly as I said it was. The Bill, as we passed it, gave the board, notwithstanding any bargain that was made with the landpwner in reference to a crossing, the right to determine whether a crossing should be given or not, whereas, the Senate amendment directs that the commissioners, if a bargain has been made that there shall be no crossing, to inquire into the circumstances of that bargain in considering the application. If

a railway company in order to be relieved from the necessity of making a railway crossing, are obliged to buy a whole farm and sell it off in sections, after making that bargain with the individuals, why should they be obliged afterwards to provide a crossing if the railway commissioners decide that it is necessary ?

I can answer my hon. friend's question. I think there would be good reason. The conditions may have changed as yearsl have gone on. The situation of the land may be different. The reasons which originally made the crossing unnecessary might not then exist and would not be at all applicable to the matters that come before the board. As the amendment of the Senate limits the jurisdiction of the board I agree with the hon. Minister of Justice that we should not concur in it.

I thought our original Bill went farther. I thought it gave a farmer the right to a crossing upon any unsold land that he had. The old Railway Act provided that a farmer was entitled to a crossing, but I think that was only one crossing to every lot. That lot might be 100 acres in extent. The case I have in mind is where a man sells the half of his lot. He has one crossing for the whole lot but that crossing happens to be on one of the fifty acre subdivisions. He sells the one which has the railway crossing. The railway runs through the centre of the farm and he wants another crossing but because the original crossing happened to be on the other fifty acres and although he is willing to bear all the expense of making a second crossing he is not allowed the right to another crossing so as to get the use of his land which he owned before the railway was put through the farm at all. It seems to me that is a very hard case, but many eases of that kind occur and I thought that in the Bill which we passed we had provided a fair means of redress for a farmer under such circumstances as those.

Under the law provision was made for farm crossings. Supposing a farmer has 100 acres. He subsequently subdivides the property. The case I have in my mind at the present moment is a case with which I was connected, the case of a father who owned 100 acres of land. He subdivided his farm so as to give one part of his property on his right to one son and another part on his left to another son, he himself reserving the middle farm. After a time the sons wanted to get a farm crossing for themselves. Application was made to the railway company, the company refused, suit was brought in the province of Quebec, it was held that they were entitled to a farm crossing for each farm, but the case was appealed to the Supreme Court, and in the Supreme Court it was decided that in view of the original purchase of the property,
a provision' being made for only one crossing, they were entitled to no more. Under the Bill as we passed it the board can authorize as many crossings as under the circumstances they think necessary. But the amendment passed by the Senate would oblige the board when application is made to take into consideration the circumstances connected with the original purchase and limit their authority to deal with it. Under these conditions we think it better that the board should be absolutely free to exercise their own judgment in regard to the conditions which exist at the time the application is made.

I think the farmer is entitled to that right. While the board is free to say that a crossing shall be provided it is equally free to say that it cannot be made and if it says that there shall be no crossing the farmer is deprived of the right" of using his land.

That would be a very good criticism of the Bill as we sent it to the Senate, but it is an absolute criticism of the amendment of the Senate which goes much further in the direction of doing what my hon. friend wants to prevent this Bill from doing.
I am entirely opposed to the amendment of the Senate. I think it is an absurdity. I thought the Act as we sent it contained a complete provision.

What would the probable cost be of taking this before the Railway Commission ? I think there should be very little trouble for a farmer to get across a railway, because we know the very great inconvenience the farmers are often put to by railways being built across their farms. The case which the Minister of Justice cited, would show that if a farmer divided his farm among his sons, they might have a great deal of difficulty in getting across it.
I would be strongly in favour of making it as easy as possible for a farmer to get across a railway without going to any great expense.

On amendment 40,

I propose that we disagree to this amendment. It is an amendment to section 211, which is called the contracting out clause. Subsection 4, of section 211, provides that the company shall be liable for damages to the individual who lias suffered injury, or to his representatives, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary with regard to auy such person. That is to say, no agreement can lie entered into between the company and the individual, which will save the company from liability in the case of an ac-

cident; that if the company is liable to the individual, and if for any consideration which they choose to give, for instance by way of insurance, they make a contract with him by which he will waive all claims against the company for the damage he may suffer, accepting in lieu of the claim such indemnity as the company may fix or determine in advance ; such an agreement as that is invalid. So far as I am personally concerned, I would like to make this statement : As to whether or not such a provision as that can be contained in a railway Act passed by the federal parliament, I am doubtful. I would like to protect myself on that score.
Doubtful whether it would invalidate the contract ?

Yes.
EIou. Mr. HAGGART. What is the effect of the Senate amendment ?

Under the English workman's Compensation Act, or the Employer's Liability Act, I forget which, for the moment; an employee can contract himself out, provided the form of contract is prepared beforehand and submitted to an official who is called the registrar of friendly societies. If it is approved of by that official, the contract is binding, and there are certain conditions as to what this agreement must contain. It seems to me that the attempt of the Senate, was to some extent, to adopt that provision, but the Senate failed entirely in that object. Their amendment was :
That after the words ' notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary with regard to any such person,' the following should be added-
Unless such agreement shall have been first approved by order or regulation of the board.
The idea would be that each time an agreement which would have for effect to restrict the liability of the company, would be entered into with a particular individual, that agreement, if submitted to the board and sanctioned by the board, should be binding. I presume the object they had in view was to substitute the board for the registrar of friendly societies in England. My difficulty is, and I will not do more than merely state it; a contract of lease and hire is essentially a civil contract under the control of the provincial legislature, and if the contract is made in the province, it is made subject to the law of that particular province, and how far we have the right to say, that an individual in a province can not enter into a contract, which is in my judgment an ordinary civil contract, is to say the least doubtful. I do not enter any dissent against this, but I wish to express my personal view, and I do so for my protection if the matter is considered nere-after.
If we reject the amendment of the Senate, will not the effect he to do away with the present insurance companies, to which the largest amount is contributed by the railway companies ?

It seems to me that will be the effect. At present each railway company contributes to the employees' liability insurance company a certain amount, and when each individual is hired by the company he signs an agreement by which he becomes a member of the insurance society, and by which he binds himself and his representatives not to claim more than a certain amount from the company. That means, that the liability of the company is limited. The consideration given by the company is a contribution towards the insurance fund. If that contract be not binding, it is presumable that the companies would not continue their contribution. However, I will not discuss that matter now. I have my individual opinion about it, but it is a matter which after all the employees who are interested in this legislation are most concerned about. If they consider it desirable to set aside these insurance benefits, that is a matter that concerns them, and I think after all they ought to be the best judges.

With respect to section 284, as to traffic agreements, is there any conflict between that and one of the sections we have already passed-I do not recall the number at the moment-providing that consent must be obtained for the pooling of receipts. The hon. member will see this expresses ali that appears in the first paragraph of section 284 in fewer words and more general terms. I think perhaps that it is an improvement, because when you elaborate the statute you are apt to forget something and so get into trouble. And the second paragraph of the amendment:
2.	The directors may also make and enter into any agreement or arrangements, not Inconsistent with the provisions of this or the special Act, for.

I am told there is a great distinction, and I endeavoured to get an explanation of it, and the explanation embarrassed me. There may have been reason for the Senate striking that out. An examination of the statutes would probably lead the Minister of Justice to see it was a reasonable amendment.
